text: The Taliban released an 11-page biography of reclusive founder Mullah Mohammed Omar to counter rumors of his death and reassert his leadership amid competition from ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi. The document, published by the Taliban's Cultural Commission, describes Omar's daily activities and early life but provides no video or audio evidence of the one-eyed fugitive, who has not been publicly seen since the U.S. routed the Taliban from Afghanistan in 2001. Analysts suggest the biography is an attempt to maintain Omar's authority over Taliban militants who may be attracted to ISIS's more visible leadership.

Hundreds mourned Walter Scott at his funeral Saturday in South Carolina, where church leaders called his fatal shooting by white police officer Michael Slager "an act of overt racism" and a catalyst for change. Slager was charged with murder after a bystander's video showed him shooting the fleeing black man in the back, though his defense may argue it was a heat-of-passion manslaughter case stemming from a reported struggle over a Taser. Scott had fled the traffic stop due to an outstanding warrant for unpaid child support.

A former TSA agent in Tennessee was sentenced to six months in jail for secretly videotaping a female co-worker in a bathroom and breaking into her home, where he collected over 90 videos and 1,500 photos. Daniel Boykin pleaded guilty to unlawful photography, aggravated burglary and computer crimes, and will serve five and a half years of probation with GPS monitoring. The judge called the invasion of privacy "egregious," and the TSA terminated Boykin when the investigation began.

Cape Verde, a 500,000-person island nation off West Africa with no oil or mineral resources, is leveraging its rich musical heritage to boost its economy through events like the Kriol Jazz Festival and Atlantic Music Expo. The government and private sector are working to give Cape Verdean artists international exposure and establish music and culture as key economic drivers, with tourism expected to account for 20% of GDP by 2024.

Arsenal beat Burnley 1-0 to move within four points of Chelsea atop the Premier League table, with a crucial clash between the two sides scheduled for next week. Aston Villa defeated Tottenham 1-0 while Leicester City upset West Brom 3-2 in relegation-zone action. Crystal Palace thrashed Sunderland 4-1 with Yannick Bolasie scoring a hat trick.

David Lynch exited Showtime's planned Twin Peaks revival over a salary dispute, saying insufficient funding prevented him from executing the script properly. The original cast, including Sheryl Lee and Peggy Lipton, launched a #SaveTwinPeaks campaign backing Lynch, arguing the revival cannot proceed without him. Showtime said it hopes to resolve the dispute and bring back the series with both Lynch and co-creator Mark Frost.

Andrew Getty, 47-year-old heir to the Getty oil fortune, died of apparent natural causes, Los Angeles police said Tuesday. The grandson of oil tycoon J. Paul Getty had "several health issues" and no foul play is suspected, though an autopsy will be conducted. Getty had recently filed for a restraining order against an ex-girlfriend, citing a serious medical condition involving dangerously high blood pressure.

A Maryland woman was arrested after allegedly abandoning her 21-year-old quadriplegic son in Philadelphia woods for over four days while visiting her boyfriend in Maryland; the man was found covered in leaves suffering from dehydration and malnutrition. The mother, Nyia Parler, cannot be extradited to face charges including aggravated assault until she completes unspecified treatment in Maryland. The son, who also has cerebral palsy and cannot communicate, was hospitalized and is being cared for by his aunts who have sought guardianship.

NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer named an asteroid after Pakistani education activist Malala Yousafzai, who survived a Taliban shooting and won the Nobel Peace Prize. Asteroid 316201 Malala, discovered by Mainzer in 2010, orbits between Mars and Jupiter every 5.5 years and is about 4 kilometers in diameter. Mainzer chose to honor Malala because few asteroids are named after women, particularly women of color, and because educating girls globally increases human potential.

A gastrointestinal illness has sickened 100 people aboard the cruise ship Celebrity Infinity, including 95 passengers and 5 crew members, according to the CDC. The cause remains undetermined, and CDC officials are scheduled to board the ship in San Diego on Monday to investigate. This is the third gastrointestinal outbreak on the vessel since 2006.

The entire "Star Wars" saga became available for digital streaming this week. Mindy Kaling's brother revealed he posed as a black man to gain admission to medical school, sparking controversy over affirmative action. A couple named Joel Burger and Ashley King received a free wedding from Burger King after the fast food chain learned of their July nuptials.

Philadelphia woman Keonna Thomas, 30, was charged Thursday with attempting to travel to Syria to join ISIS after purchasing a visa to Turkey and booking flights to Barcelona. Two New York women, Noelle Velentzas and Asia Siddiqui, were also arrested Thursday on terror charges—Velentzas and Siddiqui for allegedly planning to build an explosive device for U.S. attacks. The arrests are part of a surge in prosecutions, with the Justice Department handling more than 30 cases in 18 months of people attempting to support terrorist groups, 18 of which involve ISIS.

HBO released a teaser for "True Detective" season 2, premiering June 21, starring Colin Farrell, Vince Vaughn, Rachel McAdams and Taylor Kitsch. The new season follows three law-enforcement officers and a criminal investigating a bizarre murder amid conspiracy and betrayal in California. The critically acclaimed show's first season, starring Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson, was a major hit.

Carlos Colina, 32, was charged Monday with assault and battery and improper disposal of a body after human remains were discovered in a duffel bag in Cambridge, Massachusetts over the weekend. The remains belonged to 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien, whom Colina knew; additional body parts were found at a nearby apartment building. Authorities are awaiting medical examiner results to determine if further charges will be filed.

College basketball recruit Trey Moses asked high school freshman Ellie Meredith, who has Down syndrome, to prom at Eastern High School in Louisville, Kentucky, presenting her with flowers and a Taylor Swift reference poster. The gesture, which went viral on social media, was facilitated through the school's Best Buddies program that fosters friendships between students with and without developmental disabilities. Moses plans to major in special education while playing college basketball at Ball State.

NBC debuts "A.D. The Bible Continues," a 12-week sequel to the 2013 History Channel hit, following Jesus' resurrection and early Christianity. "Mad Men" begins its final episodes on AMC, revealing the fate of Don Draper and other characters. Netflix launches "Marvel's Daredevil," a dark drama about blind lawyer Matt Murdock who fights crime as a costumed vigilante.

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence signed a controversial religious freedom law allowing discrimination against LGBT individuals to shore up conservative credentials ahead of a potential 2016 presidential run, despite opposition from business leaders and his state's Republican mayor. The move reflects a broader push by multiple Republican-controlled states to pass similar legislation, potentially forcing 2016 GOP candidates to take hardline positions on LGBT rights during the primary. While national polling shows growing support for same-sex marriage, the political dynamics suggest cultural issues around LGBT rights will play an outsized role in the 2016 election.

Apple released new emojis with diverse skin tones, sexual orientations, and ethnicities, sparking both celebration and controversy. While the update is seen as important representation for marginalized groups in digital communication, some groups like redheads and Armenians feel excluded. The move reflects changing American demographics, though critics question why it took so long.

Avril Lavigne revealed she was bedridden for five months with Lyme disease after being bitten by a tick last spring, causing severe symptoms including inability to breathe, talk, or move. The Canadian singer recuperated at her Ontario home with support from her husband Chad Kroeger and mother while doctors initially struggled to diagnose her condition. Now 80 percent recovered, Lavigne is releasing new music and says the illness has given her a new perspective on life.

New research by the Anne Frank House indicates that Anne Frank and her sister Margot died at least a month earlier than previously believed, likely in early February 1945 rather than March 1945. Researchers re-examined Red Cross archives and survivor testimonies to conclude the sisters probably succumbed to typhus at Bergen-Belsen concentration camp before February 7, based on witness accounts of their symptoms. The timing means Anne died roughly two months before the camp's liberation in May 1945.

Two Troy University students, Ryan Calhoun and Delonte Martistee, have been arrested and charged with sexual battery following a gang rape allegation at Panama City Beach during spring break in March 2015. Video evidence of the alleged assault was discovered during an unrelated investigation and turned over to authorities. Both students have been suspended from the university, and investigators say more arrests are expected as the investigation continues.

A stray dog in Washington State survived being hit by a car, struck with a hammer in an attempted mercy killing, and buried in a field, only to stumble to a nearby farm four days later. The one-year-old bully breed mix, now named Theia, is receiving treatment at Washington State University's Veterinary Teaching Hospital for a dislocated jaw, leg injuries, and sinus damage. Her rescuer has launched a fundraising campaign that has already exceeded $10,000 to cover the dog's extensive medical procedures.

The FBI has confirmed that Malaysian bomb maker Marwan (Zulkifli bin Hir), a wanted member of Jemaah Islamiyah, was killed in a January raid in the southern Philippines. The operation resulted in 44 elite police commandos being killed and shattered a ceasefire with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, threatening a fragile peace agreement in the region. Critics argue authorities overemphasized eliminating Marwan, whose actual threat may have been exaggerated, jeopardizing peace efforts in the southern Philippines.

# Summary

A critic argues the Obama administration's nuclear framework with Iran surrenders crucial leverage by offering sanctions relief while allowing Iran to maintain its nuclear infrastructure and enrichment program. The deal lacks adequate inspection safeguards and expires too quickly, risking Iran's breakout capability within 15 years, while funding a state sponsor of terrorism supporting Assad, Hezbollah, and Houthi forces.

"Mad Men" concludes its final season Sunday after eight years as a cultural phenomenon depicting a 1960s advertising agency amid social upheaval. The show faces the challenge of sticking its landing following the moon landing finale of season six, with creator Matthew Weiner expected to navigate the latter half of 1969 and potential departures of key characters like Roger Sterling and Peggy Olson. The series has become emblematic of the era's disintegration, reflecting the collapse of old institutions and generational conflict.

Katie, a giraffe at the Dallas Zoo, gave birth to a roughly 6-foot-tall calf during a live-streamed labor Friday evening captured by 10 cameras for Animal Planet. The newborn showed positive signs including ear movement, attempts to stand, and nursing efforts. The birth followed Katie's 15-month gestation period and was witnessed by fellow giraffes including her companion Jade.

Loretta Lynch's confirmation as attorney general has stalled for six months in the full Senate after clearing the Judiciary Committee in February, longer than any previous AG nominee in recent history. Civil rights advocates and Democratic lawmakers suggest the delay is racially motivated, while Republicans deny this and cite partisan disputes over unrelated bills. Lynch's family in North Carolina, including her retired civil rights activist father, has become a focal point in the debate over her nomination.

Armed assailants attacked the attorney general's office in Balkh province, northern Afghanistan on Thursday, killing three people and wounding five others. An ongoing firefight between the attackers and Afghan security forces was underway, with most civilians evacuated. Two police officers and a security guard were among the dead.

Bob Barker, 91, made a surprise return to host "The Price Is Right" for the first time in eight years on April 1, handling the opening segment before handing duties to regular host Drew Carey. Barker, who hosted the show for 35 years before retiring in 2007, appeared sharp and seamlessly conducted the "Lucky Seven" game.

Blues legend B.B. King was hospitalized for dehydration caused by his Type II diabetes but was discharged the same day, feeling "much better." The 89-year-old guitarist returned home to rest with his grandchildren. King had previously canceled tour dates last year due to similar dehydration and exhaustion issues.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all counts in the Boston Marathon bombing. The article argues that preventing future radicalization requires understanding that extremism stems from political grievances and perceived attacks on Muslim communities worldwide, not from Islam itself. The author contends that engaged Muslim communities offering constructive alternatives to violence, rather than religious reformation, are key to countering radicalization.

A video roundup of the week's top stories includes tours of Mike Tyson's abandoned Ohio mansion, footage of the world's tallest and fastest roller coaster, and a CNN exclusive interview with Bikram yoga creator Bikram Choudhury's accusers. Other notable videos feature a shepherd's account of witnessing Germanwings Flight 9525 crash in the French Alps, Penn Jillette debating Indiana's religious freedom law, and a study on facial beauty standards.

The Pentagon reports coalition forces have retaken 25-30% of Iraqi territory from ISIS, primarily through conventional frontal assaults on the terror group's edges rather than strategic maneuver warfare. However, counterinsurgency experts warn that territorial gains alone don't indicate victory, as ISIS compensates for losses by launching spectacular attacks elsewhere to maintain its image of strength and recruitment appeal. The coalition's strategy lacks the sophisticated maneuver tactics and regional coordination that could more rapidly disrupt ISIS's command structure and supply lines.

A man attacked soccer player Oliver Minatel with his headphone cord on an Air Canada flight to Atlanta, attempting to choke him before other passengers intervened. The suspect, who claimed the soccer team was trying to kill him, was escorted off the plane upon landing and transported for mental evaluation by Atlanta police. No federal charges have been filed pending investigation.

British banker Rurik Jutting, 29, was charged with two counts of murder after Hong Kong police discovered two Indonesian women dead in his Wan Chai apartment in November—one on the floor with neck wounds, another stuffed in a suitcase on the balcony. The victims, domestic workers Seneng Mujiasih, 29, and Sumarti Ningsih, 25, were identified as having been killed days apart. A court hearing to determine if there is sufficient evidence to proceed to trial was adjourned until May pending analysis of over 200 pieces of forensic and DNA evidence.

Multiple tornadoes swept through the rural Midwest on Thursday, with a particularly destructive twister cutting a 22-mile path through Illinois's Ogle County near Rochelle and Fairdale, destroying homes and killing one person. The storm damaged or destroyed approximately 70 houses in the area, though National Weather Service warnings helped minimize casualties. The severe weather also affected Oklahoma, Kansas, Missouri, and Iowa, with hail the size of tennis balls reported in some areas.

Don McLean's handwritten manuscript of "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at Christie's auction Tuesday, the third-highest price ever paid for an American literary manuscript. The 16-page draft includes lines that didn't make the final version and extensive notes. McLean, turning 70, decided to sell the iconic 1971 song to provide for his family.

UN Relief and Works Agency Commissioner-General Pierre Krähenbühl will visit Syria's Yarmouk Palestinian refugee camp Saturday to assess the humanitarian crisis affecting 18,000 Palestinians and Syrian civilians. The camp, controlled by ISIS and al Qaeda-affiliated groups, has been devastated by fighting since 2012, with its population plummeting from 160,000 to 18,000 and largely cut off from aid since 2013. The visit aims to explore ways to relieve widespread malnutrition and medical shortages in the camp located six miles from Damascus.

Saudi-led coalition airstrikes on Yemen's capital Sanaa have killed an estimated 600 people in just over a week, with fighting destroying infrastructure and cutting electricity to 16 million residents. The Houthi rebels still control the city despite the bombing campaign, while the International Committee of the Red Cross urgently appeals for a humanitarian ceasefire and aid access. The conflict stems from Houthi rebels forcing out President Hadi in January; Saudi Arabia intervened to reinstall him, complicating an already chaotic situation worsened by al Qaeda's presence in eastern Yemen.

Richie Benaud, legendary Australian cricket captain and broadcaster, has died at 84 after battling skin cancer. Regarded as cricket's greatest commentator, Benaud captained Australia from 1958-1964 without losing a series and later spent over four decades with the BBC bringing the sport to millions worldwide. His death prompted tributes from world leaders, cricketers, and sports figures globally.

A nearly five-minute total lunar eclipse occurred early Wednesday morning across western North America, with the totality lasting just four minutes and 43 seconds—the shortest of the century. The eclipse was visible west of the Mississippi River and partially across the nation, though sunrise interrupted views on the East Coast; it was also visible in parts of South America, India, China and Russia. This is the third in a rare series of four consecutive lunar eclipses, known as a "tetrad," with the final eclipse occurring September 28.

Real estate heir Robert Durst, 71, has been federally charged with unlawful firearm possession after a .38 caliber revolver was found in his hotel room. Durst faces a maximum 10-year sentence on the weapons charge and awaits extradition to Los Angeles on a first-degree murder charge in the 2000 death of his friend Susan Berman, which could carry the death penalty. The FBI is also reviewing cold cases in multiple states where Durst lived over the past five decades.

Paul Walker, who died in a car crash in November 2013 at age 40 while filming "Fast and Furious 7," is remembered as one of Hollywood's kindest actors, with co-stars and fans paying tribute ahead of the film's release. Producers rewrote the script and used special effects and Walker's brothers as body doubles to complete the film without killing off his character, ending with an emotional tribute. The release has sparked widespread mourning, with thousands attending memorials and co-star Vin Diesel naming his newborn daughter after Walker.

On "The Price Is Right," model Manuela Arbelaez accidentally revealed the correct answer to a pricing game, inadvertently giving away a Hyundai Sonata to the contestant. Host Drew Carey laughed off the gaffe while Arbelaez attempted to hide. The incident occurred during a busy week for the show, which also featured a guest appearance by former host Bob Barker.

Thai Smile Airways unveiled a new Airbus A320 featuring "Adventure Time" characters on its exterior and interior, partnering with Cartoon Network to promote a new water park in Thailand. The themed aircraft will begin service on April 4, flying from Bangkok to Phuket.

A mother duck and her ducklings caused a stir on a Washington D.C. street Tuesday when they crossed a busy road, prompting pedestrians and CNN staff to help corral them to safety using an umbrella. The group was eventually guided to a grassy area away from traffic. CNN correspondents called the encounter extraordinary for the nation's capital.

French investigators have completed evidence collection from the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash site in the Alps, which killed all 150 people aboard on March 24. The flight data and cockpit voice recorders have been recovered, and 150 DNA profiles have been isolated from over 2,000 samples collected. Authorities have determined that co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately locked out the captain and engineered the plane's descent, and it has emerged he had concealed depression and medical leave notes indicating he was unfit for work.

Cuba attends the Summit of the Americas for the first time since 1962 after the U.S. lifted its decades-long diplomatic blockade. The two nations are negotiating to restore formal relations, though Cuba insists on being removed from the U.S. terrorism sponsor list before reopening embassies. The summit tests whether warming U.S.-Cuba ties can withstand Cuba's alliance with Venezuela, which the U.S. has criticized for human rights abuses.

Jesus preached against wealth while his ministry relied on financial support from wealthy followers, including women like Mary Magdalene and Joanna who provided resources from their own means. The Jesus community maintained a common purse and likely survived through begging, hospitality, and donations from affluent supporters despite his teachings on the perils of riches. Scholars suggest the ministry functioned at a subsistence level, with Jesus and his disciples walking, sleeping in friends' homes, and eating what was shared or caught.

California regulators ordered Pacific Gas & Electric to pay a record $1.6 billion penalty for unsafe operation of its gas transmission system, including a 2010 pipeline rupture in San Bruno that killed eight people and injured over 50 others. Most of the penalty—$850 million—will fund pipeline safety infrastructure improvements. PG&E said it has already paid over $500 million in claims to victims and replaced more than 800 miles of pipe since the explosion.

Lauren Hill, a 19-year-old Indiana basketball player who inspired millions while battling terminal brain cancer, has died. Hill achieved her dream of playing college basketball for Mount St. Joseph University after the NCAA moved up the team's opening game to accommodate her, and she went on to raise $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research before her death.

A massive fire erupted Friday morning at GE's Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky, sending thick smoke across the industrial area. Firefighters contained the blaze, which reached at least four alarms, with no reported injuries. The cause remains under investigation.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, who has been negotiating a nuclear deal with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry, received a hero's welcome upon returning to Iran. Despite his polished public image, less-known facts about Zarif include discrepancies in his official birth year, his education in the United States during Iran's revolution, and his involvement with the Alavi Foundation under federal investigation. Zarif has spent more time negotiating with Kerry than any other foreign minister as the two work toward a June 30 deadline to finalize nuclear agreement details.

A Connecticut teen forced into chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma remains in state custody despite being in remission after nearly six months of treatment, with a judge denying her motion to return home. Her attorneys argue the ruling contradicts evidence that she is no longer at imminent risk of harm, and plan to appeal. The Department of Children and Families says it will withdraw its custody order once her final chemotherapy round concludes later this month.

Computer analysis by University of Texas researchers suggests "Double Falsehood," a play published in 1728, was actually written by Shakespeare and John Fletcher over a century earlier, with publisher Lewis Theobald making only minor edits. The study analyzed word choice and linguistic patterns across works by all three authors, finding Shakespeare's signature dominated the first half and Fletcher's the second, with minimal traces of Theobald's writing. The findings could settle a long-standing scholarly debate over the play's true authorship, though some skeptics remain unconvinced.

French prosecutors deny awareness of alleged cockpit video from Germanwings Flight 9525, contradicting reports by German and French media outlets claiming to have viewed footage recovered from a phone at the crash site. Co-pilot Andreas Lubitz, accused of deliberately crashing the plane in the French Alps killing all 150 aboard, had disclosed a history of severe depression to his airline's flight training school in 2009, though he held a valid medical certificate at the time of the crash.

Emy Afalava, a decorated veteran born in American Samoa, is suing for citizenship rights despite being subject to U.S. law his entire life, arguing the 14th Amendment guarantees citizenship to all born on U.S. soil. The federal government has denied citizenship to American Samoans, a practice rooted in early 20th-century racist Supreme Court decisions that treated island territories as second-class U.S. lands. A D.C. Circuit court decision on Afalava's case could soon resolve whether American Samoans finally receive the citizenship rights granted to residents of all other U.S. territories.

Blue Bell ice cream has shut down its Broken Arrow, Oklahoma plant after listeria contamination was discovered in products from that facility, prompting a recall of specific 3-ounce servings. The contamination is linked to a Kansas hospital outbreak that killed three people, though investigations are ongoing to confirm whether Blue Bell products are the source. This marks the company's first recall in its 108-year history.

Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for an attack on Garissa University College in eastern Kenya that killed many and took hostages, marking an escalation in the Somalia-based militant group's campaign against Kenya. The attack reflects broader regional instability driven by economic inequality, poor governance, and resource competition that fuel recruitment for extremist groups. Experts warn that military responses alone cannot resolve the crisis without addressing underlying socioeconomic and political exclusion across East Africa.

A Russian SU-27 fighter jet intercepted a U.S. RC-135U reconnaissance plane over the Baltic Sea in international airspace, with the Pentagon calling the maneuver "unsafe and unprofessional." Russia claimed the U.S. aircraft had its transponder off and was flying toward its border, but U.S. officials denied the allegation. The U.S. plans to lodge a formal diplomatic complaint with Moscow over the incident.

Artist Phillip Hyman created a black-winged angel figure from reclaimed wood as a memorial to Walter Scott, an unarmed black man shot by a white police officer in North Charleston, South Carolina. The artwork has been adopted as an icon by the Black Lives Matter movement and is being displayed at protests outside City Hall. Hyman said he created the piece to mourn with Scott's family and as a statement about police violence in America.

North Charleston police officer Michael Slager was fired and charged with murder after cellphone video showed him shooting unarmed black man Walter Scott eight times in the back as Scott fled a traffic stop. Witness accounts and video evidence contradict police reports claiming Scott grabbed Slager's Taser; the witness said he never saw Scott take the weapon. Discrepancies also emerged in officers' accounts of whether CPR was performed on Scott after the shooting.

ISIS claimed Sunday it had stormed Iraq's Baiji oil refinery and controlled several buildings, though Iraqi government officials denied the assertion and said their forces maintained full control of the strategic facility. The attack, launched late Saturday, marks another militant attempt to seize the refinery, located 40 kilometers from Tikrit, which Iraqi forces recently recaptured from ISIS. CNN could not independently verify either side's claims.

Nashville's district attorney banned prosecutors from offering female sterilization in plea deals, sparking outrage over a practice that has occurred four times in five years. The article argues sterilization as voluntary punishment likely remains constitutional since defendants can waive constitutional rights, and similar deals involving male defendants have gone largely uncontested. The author suggests public outcry stems from gender bias—castration of male sex offenders has been accepted practice, while sterilization of women is now deemed shocking.

Over 25,000 people contracted Ebola in the largest epidemic in history, with more than 10,000 deaths, though new cases have declined to 30 weekly as of April. While Liberia and Sierra Leone show significant progress with surplus treatment facilities, Guinea continues to struggle with unidentified cases and unsafe burials, raising concerns about unknown transmission chains. Survivors face permanent life changes, and the outbreak has exposed critical vulnerabilities in global public health systems.

The NCAA claims it has no legal responsibility to ensure academic integrity at member institutions, contradicting its public messaging that education is paramount for student-athletes. The position emerged in response to a lawsuit from UNC athletes caught in an academic fraud scandal where thousands were funneled into fake classes over 18 years. Critics argue the NCAA's stance reveals a fundamental contradiction: the organization cannot simultaneously claim education justifies amateurism rules while disclaiming responsibility for the quality of that education.

An explosion at a paraxylene chemical plant in Zhangzhou, China injured six people and sparked a major fire Monday night. More than 600 firefighters brought the blaze under control by Tuesday morning, with no reported toxic chemical spills. The plant, which has faced public opposition over pollution concerns, experienced a similar explosion in 2013.

Officer Michael Slager shot Walter Scott in the back as he fled police in North Charleston, South Carolina; bystander video of the incident contradicts the officer's account and would likely have prevented the tragedy had Slager been wearing a body camera. The author argues that police body cameras are essential to reduce use-of-force incidents, restore public confidence in law enforcement, and expose racial bias in policing while broader social reforms are pursued. Though body cameras are not a complete solution to systemic racism in the criminal justice system, they can serve as an immediate deterrent and accountability measure.

The VII Summit of the Americas in Panama City was expected to focus on a historic handshake between President Obama and Cuban leader Raul Castro, but Venezuela's political crisis has created diplomatic tension. Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro accused the U.S. of attempting a coup and banned several American politicians from entering the country, prompting Obama to issue sanctions; Cuba has publicly sided with Maduro, complicating the summit. The dispute threatens to overshadow the U.S.-Cuba reconciliation and could fracture hemispheric unity if other Latin American leaders align with Venezuela.

A nuclear submarine undergoing repairs at Russia's Zvyozdochka shipyard caught fire when welding work ignited rubber insulation between the hull sections. The vessel was in dry dock with no ammunition, fuel, or dangerous materials aboard, and all personnel evacuated safely with no injuries reported. Officials said the fire posed no threat to people or the facility.

Tropical storm Maysak (locally called Chedeng) approached the Philippines Saturday with sustained winds over 70 mph, down from super typhoon status earlier in the week. Authorities issued warnings for flash floods and landslides, banned outdoor activities, and evacuated residents preemptively ahead of the expected Sunday landfall on Isabela province's southeastern coast. The storm is forecast to exit the Philippines by Monday.

Deion Sanders publicly called out his son on Twitter for claiming he only eats "hood doughnuts," reminding him he has a trust fund, condo and clothing line. Sanders Jr., a SMU wide receiver and aspiring rapper, had tweeted that he refuses doughnuts unless they come in a plain white box. The younger Sanders retweeted his father's rebuke without deleting it.

Guatemala faces an epidemic of gender-based violence, with nearly 10 women killed per 100,000 people and an estimated 98% of cases never reaching court, fueled by a legacy of civil war, deep-rooted machismo culture, and systemic impunity. Despite these challenges, organizations like CICAM and programs such as "Abriendo Oportunidades" are slowly changing attitudes through survivor advocacy and education, while the government has established specialized courts and task forces to address femicide. However, experts warn that international attention and immediate action remain critical as millions of women remain trapped in cycles of violence.

Police in Malegaon, India are requiring cattle owners to register their livestock with mugshots and detailed physical descriptions to enforce a new state ban on beef sales and cow slaughter. Over 100 owners have complied so far, with authorities using the database to investigate cow slaughter cases. The Maharashtra law imposes up to five years imprisonment for beef consumption or sale, prompting beef traders to strike and vow legal challenges.

Lucknow police in India have purchased four pepper-spray drones to disperse violent crowds and plan to buy a fifth, with each unit costing $9,560-$19,300. The move has drawn criticism from those concerned about suppression of free speech and those who argue authorities should pursue dialogue and mediation rather than aggressive crowd control methods. The drones, equipped with cameras and pepper spray, are set to be officially launched later this month.

Don McLean's handwritten manuscript for "American Pie" sold at Christie's for $1.2 million to an unnamed buyer. The 8½-minute 1971 song, inspired by the 1959 plane crash that killed Buddy Holly and other rock pioneers, has become an enduring American cultural touchstone ranked among the greatest songs of the 20th century.

A gang pulled off a daring heist at a London jewelry vault over Easter weekend, reminiscent of the 1971 Baker Street bank robbery—the first major physical heist in the city in over 40 years. Former Scotland Yard commander Roy Ramm explains that sophisticated criminals are typically working-class individuals motivated purely by money, relying on meticulous planning, inside information, and trusted networks to execute high-value crimes. Police will investigate possible inside involvement, analyze forensic evidence and CCTV footage, and track the movement of known criminals to solve the Hatton Garden raid.

7-Eleven is hosting its first Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day on Saturday, allowing customers to fill any personal container—from buckets to trophies—for $1.49, the price of a medium Slurpee. Containers must fit through a 10-inch hole and be sanitary. The promotion kicks off peak Slurpee season and differs from the chain's traditional Free Slurpee Day in July.

Kentucky State Senator Georgia M. Davis McIntyre, the first woman and person of color elected to the state senate in 1967, criticized Rand Paul's presidential campaign announcement, saying his message of Republican inclusion rings hollow given his record of questioning civil rights and voting rights legislation. McIntyre argued that Paul's positions on the Civil Rights Act, voting rights, education, and immigration protections demonstrate outdated views that contradict his stated goal of expanding the party's appeal to minority voters. She concluded that Paul's record disqualifies him from the presidency and that Americans deserve a leader committed to protecting democratic progress.

A passenger died Sunday when a Lamborghini crashed into a guardrail during an Exotic Driving Experience ride at Walt Disney World Speedway in Orlando. The 36-year-old victim, Gary Terry, was pronounced dead at the scene; the 24-year-old driver suffered minor injuries after losing control of the vehicle. Petty Holdings, which operates the fantasy sports car experience, expressed condolences to those involved in the accident.

Aaron Hernandez's defense rested Monday after prosecutors spent months presenting 131 witnesses in the former NFL player's trial for the 2013 murder of semi-pro player Odin Lloyd. Key evidence includes Hernandez's suspicious claim to team owner Robert Kraft that he was in a club at the time of the killing—before the time of death was publicly disclosed—and grainy video footage prosecutors say shows him holding a .45-caliber handgun minutes after Lloyd was shot. The defense challenged the prosecution's circumstantial evidence, including questioning the reliability of footprint analysis and suggesting objects in the video could be an iPad or toy gun rather than a weapon.

Chinese authorities have detained five women's rights activists, including Wu Rongrong, for planning an International Women's Day protest against sexual harassment, denying them access to lawyers and medical care. Their case must be resolved by April 13, when they face either release or formal arrest—which typically leads to conviction in China's legal system. The detentions underscore the government's broader crackdown on independent activism despite Beijing's efforts to promote women's rights internationally.

Former Maryland Gov. Martin O'Malley challenged the notion of Hillary Clinton's inevitability as a Democratic frontrunner, citing 2008 when Clinton lost to Barack Obama despite being considered the presumptive nominee. Speaking in Iowa, O'Malley suggested lesser-known candidates could gain traction by engaging voters directly. Clinton, who leads most polls by over 40 points, is set to announce her presidential campaign Sunday.

Former NFL player Aaron Hernandez was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison Wednesday for the June 2013 killing of 27-year-old Odin Lloyd. Lloyd's family members delivered emotional victim impact statements in the Fall River, Massachusetts courtroom, describing him as a devoted son, uncle and athlete who worked for a landscaping firm and played semi-pro football. Lloyd's mother told the court she forgives those responsible for her son's death.

Ted Cruz, the only official 2016 GOP presidential candidate so far, campaigned in Iowa emphasizing his evangelical Christian faith and religious freedom issues, drawing large crowds in the state known for its influential evangelical voter base. Cruz is employing a three-pronged strategy to win the nomination by appealing to evangelicals, tea party supporters, and libertarian-minded voters, with his campaign betting that mobilizing stay-at-home evangelical voters could significantly boost Republican turnout. However, Cruz faces stiff competition from other likely GOP candidates including Mike Huckabee and Rick Santorum, who won Iowa's caucuses in 2008 and 2012 respectively.

Marvel Studios and other studios released a flurry of character reveals Thursday, including Paul Bettany's Vision in "Avengers: Age of Ultron," Charlie Cox's Daredevil suit, Ben Hardy as Angel in "X-Men: Apocalypse," and Jamie Bell's CGI-rendered Thing in the "Fantastic Four" reboot. The simultaneous announcements underscore the superhero genre's continued dominance in Hollywood. Ryan Reynolds' "Deadpool" also received a new photo release during the same promotional blitz.

Italian Coast Guard rescued 978 migrants in the Mediterranean Sea off Libya on Friday, part of a surge in crossings this year. More than 10,000 migrants have arrived in Italy in the first three months of 2015, with at least 480 deaths reported—a dramatic increase from fewer than 50 deaths in the same period last year. Most migrants originate from West Africa, Somalia, and Syria, using Libya as a transit point, and often travel in overcrowded vessels operated by smugglers.

French-language broadcaster TV5Monde regained control of one of its 11 channels Thursday after a massive cyberattack Wednesday crippled its broadcasts and social media accounts. ISIS logos appeared on the network's hacked social media pages, though no group claimed responsibility. The network, which reaches 260 million homes worldwide, was gradually restoring its channels and online platforms.

David Lynch has withdrawn as director of the "Twin Peaks" revival set for 2016, citing insufficient funding from Showtime to produce the show properly. Lynch announced his departure via Twitter and personally notified the cast, though Showtime expressed hope of resolving the dispute and bringing back both Lynch and co-creator Mark Frost.

Two major trials near completion in Massachusetts: Boston Marathon bombing suspect Dzhokhar Tsarnaev faces potential death penalty on 30 charges, while former NFL player Aaron Hernandez awaits jury deliberations in a murder case. Elsewhere, Sen. Rand Paul officially announces his 2016 presidential bid in Kentucky, Chicago holds a surprising mayoral runoff between incumbent Rahm Emanuel and challenger Jesus Garcia, and Ferguson, Missouri holds elections amid ongoing tensions over police representation.

Multiple tornadoes touched down across Kansas and Missouri Wednesday night, with a twister passing near Wichita and others reported in southwestern Kansas and near Potosi, Missouri. Nighttime tornadoes posed particular danger to communities in the affected areas. Additional severe storms are expected Thursday across the Midwest and surrounding regions.

Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison without parole Monday for the 2008 murder of ex-boyfriend Travis Alexander, with the judge rejecting the possibility of early release after 25 years. Two separate juries deadlocked on whether to impose the death penalty, removing capital punishment as an option and leaving sentencing to the judge. Arias expressed remorse before sentencing while Alexander's family members delivered emotional victim impact statements.

A Delaware family was hospitalized after exposure to methyl bromide, a restricted pesticide, at a luxury villa in the U.S. Virgin Islands during a March 14-22 stay. The EPA detected the toxic chemical in the unit and is investigating whether it resulted from an unauthorized fumigation at the resort on March 18. The Department of Justice has launched a criminal investigation into the incident, with pest control company Terminix cooperating with authorities.

A Columbia Journalism School review found Rolling Stone's article about an alleged gang rape at the University of Virginia was deeply flawed due to failures in reporting, editing and fact-checking. While UVA cannot sue as a government entity, Phi Kappa Psi fraternity members may have grounds for a defamation lawsuit if they can prove the false statements caused them individualized harm and financial damages. Such cases are rare but this situation presents stronger legal footing than typical defamation claims.

FBI agents pursuing armed robbery suspect Kevone Charleston, 36, confronted him at a CVS in Georgia on Saturday morning as he attempted to commit what would have been his 33rd commercial robbery since November 2013. Charleston fled in his vehicle, ramming multiple FBI cars and injuring two agents before being shot and apprehended in the median; his injuries are non-life-threatening. The two injured agents were treated and released.

A Menzies Aviation ramp agent fell asleep in the pressurized cargo hold of Alaska Airlines Flight 448 and was discovered after banging and yelling alerted the pilot 14 minutes into the flight from Seattle to Los Angeles. The plane made an emergency landing and the employee was taken to a hospital as a precaution, passing a drug test before being discharged. Alaska Airlines is investigating how the worker ended up in the cargo hold after his team lead failed to locate him during pre-departure checks.

A judge ruled Monday that Craig Hicks, charged in the February deaths of three Muslim college students in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, is eligible for the death penalty. Hicks, 21, shot neighbors Yusor Mohammad, Deah Shaddy Barakat, and Razan Mohammad Abu-Salha in the head; authorities are investigating whether the killings were motivated by a parking dispute or hate crime. The FBI and Department of Justice have opened a parallel inquiry into potential federal hate crime violations.

Amnesty International released a report documenting widespread attacks on women's rights activists in Afghanistan by the Taliban, warlords, and government officials, with little protection from authorities. The brutal murder of Farkhunda sparked unprecedented protests where Afghan women served as pallbearers at her funeral, defying tradition and signaling a growing resistance to violence against women. Despite facing threats and inadequate government support, activists like Selay Ghaffer continue their work, viewing the moment as the beginning of an uprising for women's rights.

A New York judge authorized serving divorce papers via Facebook private messaging, marking a shift in how legal documents can be delivered. Traditional alternate service methods like "nail and mail" or publication in obscure newspapers are often unreliable, making electronic service more practical since most people maintain consistent online presence. The ruling reflects evolving legal standards that prioritize actually notifying defendants over outdated procedures.

Rev. Robert H. Schuller, founder of the Crystal Cathedral megachurch and the televised "Hour of Power" ministry, died Thursday at age 88 from esophageal cancer. The California televangelist pioneered feel-good Christianity and was among the first to broadcast Sunday services on television, reaching millions with his message of "possibility thinking." His empire later collapsed amid family succession disputes and financial troubles, leading to the church's 2010 bankruptcy.

Four workers died and 45 were injured in a massive fire on Mexico's Abkatun Permanente oil platform in the Gulf of Mexico on Wednesday. About 300 workers were evacuated as boats battled the blaze for hours before extinguishing it that night. Pemex denied the platform collapsed and said there was no oil spill, though the cause of the fire remains unknown.

Kansas Gov. Sam Brownback signed the nation's first law banning dilation and evacuation, a common second-trimester abortion procedure, with exceptions only to protect the mother's life or health. Abortion rights advocates condemned the measure as dangerous and among the most restrictive in the country, while anti-abortion groups hailed it as groundbreaking and vowed to push similar laws in other states. Both sides indicated they are prepared to challenge the law in court.

Chinese TV host Bi Fujian apologized after a video surfaced showing him cursing late Chairman Mao Zedong during a private dinner party, calling him an "old son of a b***h" while riffing on a revolutionary song. The incident sparked controversy in China, where disrespecting leaders is taboo, with critics demanding punishment while others defended him as simply joking in a private setting. State broadcaster CCTV said it would investigate the 56-year-old personality, known as "Grandpa Bi."

Kentucky guard Andrew Harrison apologized Sunday for using a racial slur caught on a hot mic after the team's loss to Wisconsin, saying his words were "in jest" and meant no disrespect toward Wisconsin's Frank Kaminsky. Kaminsky said he accepted the apology and was "over it" after the two players spoke. Harrison wished Kaminsky well ahead of Monday's national championship game against Duke.

"Arrested Development" will return for a fifth season with 17 episodes, according to executive producer Brian Grazer. Netflix has not officially confirmed the announcement. The show's full cast availability for the new season remains unclear.

The Large Hadron Collider, the world's largest particle accelerator, has restarted after a two-year shutdown and begun circulating beams following final tests. The €3 billion machine aims to recreate conditions from moments after the Big Bang to answer fundamental physics questions about mass, dark matter, and the universe's composition. Scientists hope to push the beams to record energy levels to unlock mysteries beyond the current Standard Model of particle physics.

An Iranian military observation aircraft flew within 50 yards of a U.S. Navy helicopter over the Persian Gulf in an unsafe maneuver that U.S. officials believe may have been ordered by a local Iranian commander rather than authorized by top leadership. The incident, which occurred during nuclear negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, raised concerns about potential escalation, though no shots were fired and the helicopter safely disengaged. U.S. officials are considering filing a formal protest and noted the Iranian aircraft disappeared for two weeks afterward, suggesting the local commander may have been reprimanded.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all 30 counts in the Boston Marathon bombing trial, including 17 capital charges making him eligible for the death penalty. The case will now move to a penalty phase where jurors must decide whether to execute the 21-year-old, weighing aggravating factors like the heinousness of the crimes against mitigating factors including his youth and mental health history. His defense attorney faces a difficult task convincing the jury to spare his life, given the premeditated nature of the attack and civilian casualties.

Four employees of Indian ethnic-wear chain FabIndia have been arrested after Federal Education Minister Smriti Irani discovered a security camera overlooking a changing room at a Goa store. The store manager remains at large. The arrested staff face charges of voyeurism and breach of privacy, with potential sentences of up to three years imprisonment.

Iran's deputy sports minister announced Saturday that a ban on women attending men's sports events—in place since the 1979 Islamic Revolution—will be lifted for some indoor sports in the coming year. The exact scope remains unclear, as officials say restrictions won't change for all matches. The move comes after international pressure from FIFA and others, including the ban's role in Iran losing its bid to host the 2019 Asian Cup.

Ramalinga Raju, former chairman of Indian software giant Satyam Computers Services, has been sentenced to seven years in jail along with nine others for their roles in a $1.6 billion fraud case involving inflated profits and fictitious assets. The 2009 scandal, compared to the Enron case, devastated the fourth-largest Indian software services provider and its investors. Raju, who founded Satyam in 1987, was also fined $804,000.

Elizabeth Sedway, a cancer patient, was removed from an Alaska Airlines flight in Hawaii after an employee reported she seemed weak, despite having no doctor's note clearing her to fly. The airline apologized and refunded her tickets and hotel costs, but Sedway missed her chemotherapy appointment and her family missed school and work as a result of the incident.

Kayahan, one of Turkey's most beloved singers and songwriters, died Friday of cancer at age 66. The guitarist and composer, who achieved fame after releasing his 1991 album "I Made a Vow," had battled cancer multiple times since 1990. Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu mourned his loss, noting his significant contributions to Turkish music.

Israeli PM Netanyahu criticized the Iran nuclear deal framework, arguing for a "third alternative" of increased pressure rather than accepting what he called a "bad deal" or risking war. The deal would lift Western sanctions on Iran in exchange for reducing its centrifuges and increasing inspections, but Netanyahu contended Iran cannot be trusted and the agreement leaves too much nuclear infrastructure intact. Democrats defended the framework as a workable opportunity, while Republicans argued a future president could negotiate better terms.

A shooting spree in Washington Thursday began with a domestic kidnapping and escalated into gunfire at the Census Bureau headquarters and multiple locations across the city. A guard was critically wounded at the Census Bureau, and an officer and suspect were injured during a shootout following a police chase that ended in a crash on H Street. Police say the kidnapping victim was recovered safely and believe a single suspect was responsible for all incidents.

Chelsea Manning, imprisoned for leaking classified documents, has joined Twitter and will dictate tweets via phone to a communications firm since she lacks internet access in prison. Manning, serving a 35-year sentence, has nearly 26,000 followers and says she wants the account to be a two-way conversation. The Fort Leavenworth prison has authorized hormone therapy for Manning, who was convicted in 2013 of stealing and disseminating 750,000 pages of documents to WikiLeaks.

Rapper Nelly was arrested in Tennessee on drug charges after state troopers stopped his tour bus and found methamphetamine, marijuana, drug paraphernalia, and multiple handguns. The 40-year-old was charged with felony drug possession, simple marijuana possession, and possession of paraphernalia. He posted bond and was released from jail.

A Delaware family fell ill during a U.S. Virgin Islands vacation, possibly from methyl bromide pesticide exposure at their rented villa; the father is stable while his two teenage sons remain in critical condition. The EPA confirmed the presence of the restricted pesticide at the resort, which is banned for indoor use in the U.S. due to its acute toxicity and neurotoxic effects. The Department of Justice has launched a criminal investigation into how the odorless chemical was applied in a residential area.

Online bloggers and citizen journalists across Asia face escalating threats from both governments and violent extremists seeking to silence dissent. Authorities in Singapore, Malaysia, Vietnam, and China use legal penalties, imprisonment, and surveillance to suppress online criticism, while in Bangladesh, bloggers critical of Islam have been murdered with near-total impunity. The lack of traditional media access in authoritarian countries has made the internet a crucial platform for dissidents, but also an increasingly dangerous one.

Nina Dobrev announced she is leaving "The Vampire Diaries" at the end of season six, saying she always envisioned Elena's story as a six-season arc. Many fans expressed anger and sadness over the decision, particularly upset that the show will continue into season seven without her, potentially leaving her character's romance with Damon Salvatore unresolved. Producer Julie Plec said the show will continue focusing on the Salvatore brothers and ensemble cast.

ISIS fighters stormed the Palestinian refugee camp of Yarmouk near Damascus in April, prompting Syrian government bombing and shelling that has devastated the already war-torn area. The population has plummeted from over 100,000 to roughly 18,000 residents, who face severe shortages of food, water and medicine while trapped between pro-government forces outside and anti-regime groups inside. International aid organizations have minimal access to deliver assistance to the besieged civilians caught in the grinding urban conflict.

NASA scientists outline plans to search for extraterrestrial life over the next decade, with an estimated 40 billion Earth-like planets in habitable zones across the Milky Way. While primitive life forms may be common, intelligent civilizations capable of communication are likely rare due to the vast timescales required for their development and the short duration of their technological capabilities. Advanced telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope will search for biosignatures in exoplanet atmospheres, though meaningful contact with alien civilizations remains highly improbable.

A 32-year-old Massachusetts man faces murder charges after human remains were found in a duffel bag in Cambridge on Saturday. Carlos Colina was identified as a suspect through surveillance video, leading police to discover additional body parts at an apartment building; the remains belonged to 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien, who knew Colina. Colina is scheduled for arraignment April 14 and was previously charged with assault, battery and improper disposal of a body.

Kanye West has settled a civil lawsuit with paparazzi photographer Daniel Ramos, whom he assaulted at LAX in 2013, with West issuing a public apology and the two shaking hands. The settlement came days before trial was set to begin; West had previously pleaded no contest to misdemeanor battery and was sentenced to probation, anger management and community service. Photographer's attorney Gloria Allred said the case "sent an important message" that celebrities are not above the law.

President Obama's political investment in an Iran nuclear deal has weakened the U.S. negotiating position, making America appear more desperate than Iran despite Tehran's economic hardship from sanctions. The framework agreement announced falls far short of Obama's stated goal of Iran ending its nuclear program, instead allowing Iran to retain thousands of centrifuges and maintain most of its nuclear infrastructure while sanctions are lifted almost immediately. Critics argue the deal provides Iran political cover while failing to adequately prevent nuclear proliferation or regional instability.

A white police officer in South Carolina was arrested for murder after video evidence contradicted his account of shooting an unarmed black man, Walter Scott. The incident highlights a broader problem: a 1994 federal law requiring comprehensive data collection on police killings has never been properly implemented, leaving the nation without reliable statistics on how often such incidents occur. Without mandatory reporting, media investigations and activist websites provide only fragmented information about police violence in America.

Five Americans exposed to Ebola in Sierra Leone have been released from a Nebraska hospital after three weeks of monitoring, with none developing the virus. They were clinicians for an aid group who had contact with a colleague now being treated at the National Institutes of Health in fair condition. The CDC expects to release the last of 17 monitored patients by Thursday.

Mark Ronson's "Uptown Funk!" featuring Bruno Mars extends its reign atop the Billboard Hot 100 to 13 weeks, becoming the longest-leading song of the 2010s and just the 10th single ever to spend at least 13 weeks at No. 1. The track maintains strong performance across all metrics—digital sales, radio airplay and streaming—while Natalie La Rose's debut hit "Somebody" enters the top 10 at No. 10.

April 8, 2015 marked "Rex Manning Day," celebrating the 1995 film "Empire Records" alongside the "Lost" fan phenomenon. The article highlights other iconic dates immortalized in popular films, including April 14 from "Titanic," April 25 from "Miss Congeniality," October 3 from "Mean Girls," and October 21, 2015 from "Back to the Future Part II."

"Grace of Monaco," starring Nicole Kidman as Princess Grace Kelly, will premiere on Lifetime on May 25 after poor international box office performance. The critically-panned film, which debuted at Cannes last year, was pulled from theatrical release by The Weinstein Co., which acquired U.S. distribution rights. The movie faced controversy over its final cut, historical accuracy complaints from Grace's family, and scheduling delays before landing on the cable network.

Tokyo's Shibuya ward passed an ordinance Wednesday allowing same-sex couples to register for "partnership certificates" granting limited rights including hospital visitation and co-signing tenancy agreements, though not full marriage equality. The non-binding certificates, to be issued later this summer, represent a significant symbolic step in socially conservative Japan, where support for gay marriage among young adults reaches 70% despite overall opposition at 52.4%. Gay rights activists and lawmakers called the move a crucial first step toward marriage equality, though they emphasized that national legislation would be needed to achieve full equal rights.

California's historic four-year drought is driving up grocery prices nationwide, with berries, grapes, and other produce rising significantly in cost since the state produces over a third of U.S. vegetables and two-thirds of fruits and nuts. Gov. Jerry Brown mandated a 25% water cutback, and while a strong dollar and low oil prices may offset some price increases this year, farmers' planting decisions could still impact supermarket costs. The Western drought also drove beef prices up 12.1% in 2014, though California wine production has paradoxically improved.

University of Michigan will screen "American Sniper" after reversing its cancellation decision, despite a petition from over 200 students who objected to the film's portrayal of the Iraq War. The university's vice president said canceling the movie conflicted with the school's commitment to freedom of expression. An alternative screening of "Paddington" will be offered for students who prefer not to attend.

The 2015 MTV Movie Awards featured standout moments including Amy Schumer's sharp opening monologue, Channing Tatum twerking for Jennifer Lopez, and a surprise kiss between Schumer and Amber Rose. The show also had several misfires, including Schumer's failed archery gag, an awkward "Gone Girl" joke about Latinas, and a rambling acceptance speech from Shailene Woodley.

A section of fiberglass boat suspected to have drifted from Japan's 2011 earthquake and tsunami was found off Oregon's coast and towed to Newport this week. The debris contained live yellowtail jack fish native to Japanese waters that survived the 4,000-mile journey over four years. Scientists determined the invasive species posed minimal ecological threat, and the fish will be transferred to the Oregon Coast Aquarium.

On April 14-15, 2014, Boko Haram militants kidnapped 276 schoolgirls from Chibok, Nigeria; about 50 escaped, but over 200 remain missing one year later. President-elect Muhammadu Buhari marked the anniversary Tuesday, pledging aggressive action against the jihadist group that opposes Western education. The abductions sparked global outrage with the #BringBackOurGirls campaign, though Boko Haram continues to control parts of northeastern Nigeria and abduct civilians.

Easter's Holy Week, culminating in the Easter Triduum (Good Friday through Easter Sunday), commemorates Jesus's crucifixion and resurrection while embodying a universal human pattern of suffering, transition, and renewal. The article explains that Christians experience this three-day cycle repeatedly throughout life—moments of darkness and loss followed by transformation and hope—making Easter's spiritual significance extend beyond a single calendar date. Unlike Christmas, Easter resists commercialization because it addresses fundamental aspects of the human condition that remain deeply meaningful to believers and non-believers alike.

Kenya froze 86 accounts linked to Al-Shabaab supporters following the militant group's massacre of 147 people at a Garissa university. The government is tracking terror financing and launched airstrikes against Al-Shabaab camps in Somalia, while offering a $215,000 reward for information on the attack's alleged organizer. Kenyans mourned the victims—mostly students—at a memorial service in Nairobi as authorities faced criticism over the delayed response to the siege.

Chinese-American entrepreneur Jia Jiang launched a "100 Days of Rejection" project to overcome his fear of rejection after his tech startup failed to secure funding. The project, which included viral moments like requesting Olympic-ring donuts from a Krispy Kreme manager, led to a book deal and speaking engagements, with Jiang now advocating that people embrace rejection as an opportunity rather than an obstacle.

Attorney General Eric Holder issued a memo Friday prohibiting all Justice Department personnel, including FBI and DEA agents, from soliciting prostitutes anywhere, even in jurisdictions where it's legal, citing links to human trafficking. The directive follows an inspector general report documenting DEA agents attending sex parties paid for by drug cartels while stationed abroad. Violations will result in suspension or termination.

A Wayne Community College employee in North Carolina was shot and killed by a coworker Monday in what authorities are investigating as a possible hate crime; the victim, Ron Lane, was gay and the suspect, Kenneth Morgan Stancil III, had been terminated from a work-study program in March. Stancil fled on a motorcycle and was arrested Tuesday morning on a beach in Daytona, Florida, after traveling roughly 550 miles. Investigators are examining whether Stancil, who has facial tattoos, is affiliated with a white supremacist gang.

Governments worldwide increasingly used capital punishment in 2014 to combat terrorism and crime, including China's mass sentencing in Xinjiang and Pakistan's resumption of civilian executions following the Taliban school attack. Despite this troubling trend, global executions dropped to 607 in 2014 from 778 the previous year, with 140 countries now abolitionist in law or practice. Amnesty International argues there is no evidence that execution deters crime more effectively than imprisonment.

A Duke University student admitted to hanging a noose from a tree near campus and has been removed from school pending conduct review. The incident prompted hundreds of students and faculty to march in protest, with university President Richard Brodhead condemning it as unacceptable. Criminal investigations are ongoing and officials are determining if others were involved in the racist act.

Richard Dysart, the Emmy-winning actor best known for playing senior partner Leland McKenzie on NBC's "L.A. Law" (1986-1994), has died at 86. Dysart won an Emmy in 1992 for the role and appeared in every episode of the acclaimed legal drama. He also had a prolific career in film and television, frequently portraying authority figures and doctors in classics like "The Thing," "Wall Street" and "Being There."

Easter's date shifts annually based on the lunar calendar—specifically, the first Sunday after the first full moon following the spring equinox—a rule established by Christian bishops in 325 A.D. The holiday's secular traditions, including Easter eggs and the Easter bunny, likely originated in 17th-century Germany, possibly stemming from farmers' surplus of preserved eggs during Lent. Pope Francis marked Easter Sunday at the Vatican with calls for peace in global conflicts.

Comedian Chris Rock tweeted about being stopped by police three times in seven weeks, highlighting racial disparities in traffic stops that disproportionately affect Black drivers. The posts sparked debate on social media, with some praising his documentation of the issue and others, including actor Isaiah Washington, suggesting he adapt his behavior—such as driving less expensive cars—to avoid profiling. Rock's commentary reflects ongoing frustration over police treatment of Black Americans, particularly following high-profile deaths like those of Eric Garner and Michael Brown.

Robert Lewis Burns Jr., original drummer for Southern rock band Lynyrd Skynyrd, died Friday in a single-vehicle crash in Cartersville, Georgia at age 64. Burns was an unrestrained passenger when his car hit a mailbox and tree shortly before midnight. He had left the band in 1975 before its third album and was not involved in the 1977 plane crash that killed three members including lead singer Ronnie Van Zant.

A viral photo of a cat on stairs has sparked social media debate over whether the animal is going up or down, similar to the #TheDress phenomenon. The image, uploaded to Imgur and shared via 9gag, has divided users who disagree on the cat's direction of movement and stair construction. Brands are already capitalizing on the trending #UporDown hashtag.

The U.S. and five other world powers reached a framework agreement with Iran in Lausanne that significantly restricts Iran's nuclear program and effectively prevents it from building a nuclear weapon. The deal includes reduced uranium stockpiles, fewer centrifuges, and permanent IAEA inspection provisions, exceeding initial expectations. Critics' claims that the agreement contains fatal flaws—including sunset clauses, covert weapons programs, and insufficient restrictions—are contradicted by experts and the deal's actual terms.

Rolling Stone retracted a sexual assault story Sunday, but the underlying issue remains: University of Virginia has never expelled a student for sexual assault despite expelling 183 for honor code violations. The retraction threatens to undermine broader conversations about campus rape culture and may discourage survivors from coming forward, though investigations into UVA's handling of assault allegations continue.

Indiana Pacers forward Chris Copeland was stabbed outside a New York nightclub early Wednesday; a suspect was arrested and charged. Two Atlanta Hawks players, Pero Antic and Thabo Sefolosha, were arrested on obstruction and disorderly conduct charges after interfering with police at the scene, though they were not involved in the stabbing. Copeland suffered stab wounds to his abdomen and elbow and is in stable condition.

Twisted Sister announced its 2016 tour will be its final, marking the band's 40th anniversary with a farewell titled "Forty and F*ck It." The band will tour with new drummer Mike Portnoy, replacing A.J. Pero who died in March, and will perform two tribute shows in Pero's honor.

Actor John Travolta dismissed HBO's critical documentary "Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief," saying he hasn't seen it and doesn't plan to, calling it the work of disgruntled former members. Travolta, one of Scientology's most prominent celebrity members, credited the church with helping him survive his son's death and called the organization "brilliant." He argued he has had only positive experiences with Scientology over 40 years and wouldn't validate claims he hasn't personally experienced.

"Furious 7" earned a record $146 million over its opening weekend, with audiences emotionally moved by its tribute to late actor Paul Walker, who died in 2013 before completing filming. Filmmakers used body doubles, CGI and Walker's brothers to finish his scenes, ultimately choosing to retire his character Brian peacefully rather than kill him off. The film's ending, featuring a montage of Walker scenes set to "See You Again" by Wiz Khalifa and Charlie Puth, resonated deeply with viewers who praised it as a sincere and elegant farewell.

"Game of Thrones" season five premieres Sunday in 170 countries simultaneously, with major story arcs converging as Stannis arrives at the Wall and Tyrion's path crosses with Daenerys'. The show is moving beyond the published books and building toward a crescendo, with focus on characters like Arya, Sansa, and Cersei, while exploring what happens when common people rebel against the endless wars of nobles.

# Summary

The article profiles several remarkable cases of people surviving extended periods at sea through ingenuity and luck, including a South Carolina sailor rescued after his boat capsized multiple times, a Mexican fisherman adrift for over a year in the Pacific, a Hawaiian fisherman found after 12 days, a Panamanian teenager who survived 26 days, and a Japanese man rescued from tsunami debris. These rare survival stories contrast sharply with the far higher number of maritime deaths, highlighting the exceptional circumstances and resourcefulness required to endure such ordeals.

The first six "Star Wars" films are being released in digital HD on Friday with extensive special features. The bonus content includes behind-the-scenes footage focusing on the movies' sound design, with sound designer Ben Burtt explaining how animal sounds were used to create alien creatures like the Geonosians from "Episode II."

A jury found Dzhokhar Tsarnaev guilty on all 30 counts for the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing that killed three people and wounded hundreds of others. Survivors and victims' families expressed relief at the verdict while acknowledging that no verdict can fully compensate for their losses, with many viewing it as an important step toward closure and moving forward. The Boston community, united under the "Boston Strong" mantra, reaffirmed its resilience following the conviction.

China's former security chief Zhou Yongkang, a former member of the Communist Party's top decision-making body, has been formally charged with bribery, abuse of power, and leaking state secrets—making him the highest-ranking party official ever to face such charges. Zhou, who controlled police and spy agencies until his 2012 retirement, allegedly accumulated enormous wealth and abused his position; his case will be tried in Tianjin. His prosecution is seen as a major moment in President Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign and a demonstration of Xi's political power to hold even top-tier former leaders accountable.

A Philadelphia mother was arrested after allegedly abandoning her 21-year-old quadriplegic son with cerebral palsy in Cobbs Creek Park for over four days while she visited her boyfriend in Maryland. The man was found suffering from dehydration, malnutrition, and other injuries; his mother now faces multiple charges including aggravated assault, kidnapping, and neglect. Police say the man's aunts had offered to care for him, making the abandonment unnecessary.

Major U.S. corporations including Walmart, Apple, and NASCAR have publicly opposed religious freedom bills in Arkansas and Indiana, warning they could enable discrimination against LGBTQ individuals. Walmart's stance in its home state of Arkansas proved decisive, prompting Gov. Asa Hutchinson to pledge to veto the legislation unless revised. The corporate backlash reflects shifting American attitudes on gay rights and signals that major businesses now view LGBTQ equality as economically beneficial.

A lapsed Catholic describes how Pope Francis's compassionate approach to faith—including his non-judgmental stance on homosexuality and emphasis on welcoming sinners—has rekindled her belief after years of alienation from the Church. The author credits the Pope's focus on Jesus's message of love over rigid rules and judgment for making her feel the Church is now an "open heart" rather than a place of rejection. She plans to return to Mass for the first time in decades.

Mary Kay Letourneau, a former teacher who served seven years in prison for an affair with her 13-year-old student Vili Fualaau, says she and Fualaau remain happily married ahead of their 10th wedding anniversary. The couple, now 53 and 31 respectively, will discuss their relationship in an ABC "20/20" interview, where Letourneau plans to reveal her intentions to teach again and seek removal of her sex offender status.

Hillary Clinton's 2016 presidential campaign will inevitably become a barometer for gender equality in America, burdening her with expectations no male candidate faces. A victory risks creating complacency about women's broader political underrepresentation, while a loss could discourage future female candidates by perpetuating myths about women's electability. However, the author argues that partisan affiliation and economic conditions—not gender—will ultimately determine the election outcome, making extrapolations about women in politics from Clinton's experience inherently flawed.

Amnesty International reports that governments worldwide are increasingly using the death penalty under the guise of fighting terrorism, citing examples from Pakistan and China. While global executions fell 22% in 2014 to 607 cases, death sentences surged 28% to 2,466, driven by mass sentencings in Egypt and Nigeria. The U.S. remains among the world's top executioners alongside Iran, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia, with China estimated to execute thousands annually.

Japan's Defense Minister Gen Nakatani told parliament that the country's Air Self-Defense Force has never encountered extraterrestrial UFOs, responding to a question from former wrestler-turned-politician Antonio Inoki. Nakatani said fighter jets have occasionally been scrambled for unidentified objects, but these have only been birds or earthly aircraft. Inoki, a WWE star and North Korea wrestling diplomat, claims to have personally witnessed a UFO but acknowledged uncertainty about alien existence.

Mark Wahlberg will star in "Patriots' Day," a CBS Films production about the Boston Marathon bombing and subsequent manhunt, playing retired Boston Police Commissioner Ed Davis. The film will be told from Davis' perspective and will incorporate research and footage from CBS News' "60 Minutes." This is the second film announced about the bombing, following Fox's "Boston Strong."

Former Maryland Gov. Martin O'Malley and ex-Virginia Sen. Jim Webb, both considering 2016 Democratic presidential bids, displayed starkly different campaign styles at an Iowa Democratic event Friday—O'Malley working the room with handshakes and selfies while Webb remained reserved and biographical in his approach. Both long-shot candidates face steep odds against frontrunner Hillary Clinton, polling at just 1-3% among Democrats. Webb emphasized governance and criminal justice reform, while O'Malley delivered applause-line-heavy rhetoric about the American Dream and workers' wages.

Nine British citizens, including four children, were arrested at the Turkey-Syria border Wednesday while allegedly attempting to cross illegally into Syria. Turkish authorities did not disclose their motives, though the arrests come amid concerns about Westerners joining ISIS and other militant groups in the Syrian conflict. The British Foreign Office said it is seeking information from Turkish authorities about the incident.

The Department of Justice indicted FedEx on 15 counts related to transporting illegally prescribed pharmaceuticals, arguing the company knew it was delivering drugs from illegal internet pharmacies. FedEx argues it qualifies for a "common carrier" exemption under drug laws, which protects transportation companies from liability for contraband they unknowingly carry as part of normal business operations.
