The case raises questions about whether corporations should face criminal prosecution and whether holding delivery services liable for packages' contents makes legal or practical sense.

Al-Shabaab terrorists killed 147 people, mostly students, in an attack on Garissa University College in Kenya, making it the nation's deadliest attack since the 1998 U.S. Embassy bombing. Kenyans used social media to share victims' stories and honor the dead, while churches held emotional Easter services with armed security. One of the attackers was identified as the son of a government official from Mandera.

Swedish photographer Johan Bavman is documenting fathers taking full parental leave in Sweden, which offers 480 days total—390 paid at 80% salary—with 60 mandatory "daddy months" to encourage equal parenting. Despite the generous policy, only 12% of Swedish couples equally share leave, with women still primarily staying home. Bavman aims to photograph 60 fathers to highlight both the joys and exhaustion of full-time parenting, challenging centuries of unrecognized maternal labor.

President Obama pledged to maintain Israel's military superiority over Iran and promised U.S. support if Israel faces attack, addressing Prime Minister Netanyahu's concerns about the nuclear deal with Iran. Under the framework agreement, Iran would reduce centrifuges and allow increased inspections in exchange for sanctions relief. Obama argued the deal is worthwhile even if Iran cannot be trusted, as it provides transparency and prevents nuclear weapons development.

Indiana's new Religious Freedom Restoration Act has sparked national debate over whether such laws protect religious exercise or enable discrimination against gay people. Twenty states now have versions of religious liberty laws modeled on the 1993 federal RFRA, though legal victories under these statutes remain rare and have mostly benefited religious minorities rather than Christian denominations. The article details several cases arising from federal and state religious freedom laws, including disputes over Native American eagle feathers, a Brazilian church's sacramental tea, kosher prison meals, and a Sikh employee's ceremonial sword.

Five Chinese feminists detained before International Women's Day face charges of "assembling a crowd to disturb public order," which carries a maximum five-year prison sentence. The women, members of China's Women's Rights Action Group, were planning to distribute stickers against sexual harassment and had previously campaigned on domestic violence and women's rights issues. Their detention has drawn international criticism, including from Hillary Clinton, with human rights groups saying the activists were engaged in lawful protest.

Selena's family is creating a digital hologram of the late Tejano star that will sing, dance and interact with fans using new technology from Nevada-based company Acrovirt LLC. The project, called "Selena the One," will release new music and collaborate with current artists, with plans to tour in 2018. The family is launching an Indiegogo campaign seeking $500,000 to support the initiative.

Former Rep. Michele Bachmann compared President Obama's Iran nuclear deal to co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately crashing Germanwings Flight 9525, saying Obama was "flying his entire nation into the rocks." The comparison drew widespread criticism on social media, with commenters calling it moronic, disrespectful and a desperate bid for relevance. Bachmann has long opposed Obama's Iran negotiations, previously telling the president to "bomb Iran" at a 2014 White House Christmas party.

Ryan Gosling's directorial debut "Lost River," which premiered at Cannes a year ago to mixed reviews, finally receives theatrical release on April 10. The film began as Gosling's personal project documenting Detroit's decaying Brewster-Douglass Projects before they were demolished, evolving into a post-industrial gothic narrative about families struggling to survive urban decay. While depicting the city's destruction and abandonment, Gosling emphasizes the film also captures Detroit's resilience and ongoing rebirth through community efforts and urban renewal.

A 19-year-old UK national was arrested at Luton airport Tuesday upon returning from Turkey and charged with terror offenses. Yahya Rashid faces charges of preparing terrorist acts and assisting others in committing terrorism between November and March. He is scheduled to appear in Westminster Magistrates' Court Wednesday.

Vince Neil's recent rendition of the national anthem at a Las Vegas arena football game joined a long list of infamous celebrity performances of "The Star-Spangled Banner," ranging from Whitney Houston's celebrated 1991 Super Bowl version to Roseanne Barr's booed 1990 performance that drew presidential criticism. The article notes that performing the anthem is a high-stakes endeavor for famous musicians, with past controversial versions including Jimi Hendrix's psychedelic 1969 Woodstock take and Michael Bolton's 2003 performance marred by apparent lyrical errors.

Nearly 2,000 World War I soldiers' names and inscriptions have been discovered carved into the walls of an underground city near Naours, France, dating back almost a century. The site, which extends for miles and was used as a refuge by troops during WWI, remained largely unknown until the land changed hands in 2013 and a consortium of villages began promoting its historical significance. Photographer Jeff Gusky has documented 1,821 names—about 40% Australian, with the remainder mostly British and American—providing a poignant human connection to soldiers who often died shortly after leaving their marks.

The Palestinian Authority became the 123rd member of the International Criminal Court on Wednesday, granting the court jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories since June 2014. The move, opposed by Israel and the United States, opens the door for possible war crimes investigations against Israelis, though Palestinians may also face counter-charges. The ICC's preliminary examination will review evidence on both sides to determine whether to launch formal investigations.

Anthony Ray Hinton was released Friday after nearly 30 years on Alabama's death row for murders he did not commit; a judge dismissed charges after firearms experts determined the gun he was accused of using could not be matched to evidence in the 1985 killings of two restaurant managers. Hinton, who was 29 at the time and always maintained his innocence, said prosecutors should have tested the gun years earlier, and the Equal Justice Initiative cited race, poverty and inadequate legal representation as factors in the miscarriage of justice. The state declined to re-prosecute the case after the 2014 order for a new trial.

Eight out of ten American taxpayers receive an average $3,000 refund, creating a positive "happy ending" that overshadows the complexity and unfairness of the U.S. tax system. Free tax-filing services capitalize on this goodwill by offering add-on financial products to grateful consumers. The article argues this psychological phenomenon distracts Americans from deeper tax inequities that favor the wealthy and penalize wage earners and dual-income families.

Jordan Spieth maintained a commanding four-shot lead heading into Sunday's final round at the 2015 Masters after a steady third-round performance, despite a double bogey at the 17th hole. McIlroy, Woods, Mickelson and Rose all made moves on "Moving Day" but failed to significantly close the gap on the 21-year-old leader. Spieth's 15 birdies through three rounds put him on pace to break scoring records at Augusta.

Liana Barrientos, 39, has been married 10 times since 1999 and is facing criminal charges for submitting false information on a 2010 marriage license application. Prosecutors allege the marriages were part of an immigration scam in which some of her husbands filed for permanent residence shortly after marrying her, with divorces following only after approval. She pleaded not guilty and faces up to four years in prison if convicted.

Memories Pizza in Indiana faced backlash after owners said they'd refuse to cater same-sex weddings, sparking boycott calls and online harassment including death threats. Supporters rallied to their defense, raising over $842,000 through a GoFundMe campaign. The incident highlights the contentious debate over the state's Religious Freedom Restoration Act and its potential to allow discrimination against LGBTQ individuals.

Mindy Kaling's brother Vijay Chokalingam claims he fraudulently applied to medical school as a Black applicant to expose what he views as unfair affirmative action advantages, receiving 11 interview invitations but only one acceptance to a mid-tier school. The article argues his stunt ignores both the real discrimination minorities face and the legitimate purpose of affirmative action in addressing severe underrepresentation of minority physicians, while noting the irony that his famous sister benefited from a diversity program early in her career.

Antarctica recorded a temperature of 63.5 degrees Fahrenheit (15.5 Celsius) on March 24 at Argentina's Esperanza Base, possibly the highest ever recorded on the continent. The World Meteorological Organization is assembling a committee of climatologists to verify the measurement by examining equipment, procedures and surrounding station records. An official determination is expected by late summer or early fall.

U.S. officials have abandoned previous timelines for an Iraqi-led offensive to retake Mosul from ISIS, saying the operation could happen "soon" or "some time from now." While Iraqi forces have made progress elsewhere, including recapturing Tikrit, officials stress that retaking Mosul—a city of about a million people and a major ISIS stronghold—will be a complex, lengthy operation requiring significant military capacity.

Irish betting company Paddy Power deleted a tweet comparing Newcastle's losses to Liverpool with police violence against unarmed African-American men, calling it a joke while drawing widespread social media condemnation. Liverpool defeated Newcastle 2-0 at Anfield on Monday, with goals from Raheem Sterling and Joe Allen, moving the team to fifth place in the Premier League. The incident is the latest in a series of controversial publicity stunts by Paddy Power, which previously funded David Ginola's failed FIFA presidency bid and offered betting odds on Oscar Pistorius's trial.

Philadelphia police charged Nyia Parler, 41, with attempted murder after she allegedly abandoned her quadriplegic 21-year-old son in woods for over four days while visiting her boyfriend in Maryland. The man, who also has cerebral palsy, was found Friday suffering from dehydration, malnutrition, and exposure to freezing temperatures. Parler is in Maryland receiving unspecified treatment before extradition to Philadelphia to face additional charges including aggravated assault and reckless endangerment.

Kim Ki-Jong has been charged with attempted murder, assault on a foreign envoy, and business obstruction for stabbing U.S. Ambassador Mark Lippert in Seoul on March 5. Lippert suffered a 10-centimeter gash to his face requiring 80 stitches and cuts to his arm, but is expected to recover without permanent damage. Police say Kim, who has a history of violence and visited North Korea seven times, attacked Lippert with a 10-inch knife to protest joint South Korean-U.S. military drills.

Jill Duggar Dillard, star of TLC's "19 Kids and Counting," gave birth Monday to a 9-pound, 10-ounce son named Israel David, making her the first daughter from the show to become a mother. The baby arrived more than a week past his due date. Jill's brother Josh already has three children with a fourth on the way.

"Furious 7" is projected to open with $135-$138 million domestically this weekend, the largest North American opening since fall 2013, with a possible worldwide debut approaching $300 million. The final film featuring late actor Paul Walker is receiving Universal's widest release ever across 4,003 domestic theaters and more than 10,500 international screens. The movie's massive box office performance is driven by the franchise's popularity and public interest surrounding Walker's death in 2013.

A Secret Service supervisor was placed on administrative leave after a female employee accused him of sexual assault at an agency party, telling him she wasn't interested in his advances and later resisting his attempt to kiss her in the office. The incident marks another scandal for the agency, which has faced multiple high-profile missteps in recent months including security lapses at the White House and management failures. Director Joe Clancy called the allegations "very disturbing" and said workplace violence is unacceptable.

Hillary Clinton announces her 2016 presidential candidacy with strong credentials in political experience, though she faces challenges including questions about authenticity, connecting with the Democratic base, and avoiding the perception of inevitability that plagued her 2008 campaign. She must articulate a compelling vision on issues like financial regulation, inequality, and foreign policy while contending with gender bias and potential complications from her husband's involvement in campaigning.

The DOJ will negotiate reforms with Ferguson following findings of racial discrimination by police and courts that preyed on residents through illegal stops, excessive force, and predatory fines. Recent leadership changes—including the police chief's resignation and election of two black city council members—signal the beginning of reform, but activists must remain engaged to ensure meaningful structural change rather than superficial fixes.

Etihad Airways lost a 2-year-old cat named Felix after a flight from Abu Dhabi to New York on April 1, when the pet's damaged carrier broke open at Kennedy Airport. The airline is investigating and has hired specialists to search for the missing cat, while the owner criticizes the airline's pet handling procedures. A detection dog and wildlife traps have been deployed to help locate Felix.

A 37-year-old unemployed truck driver was rescued after drifting at sea for 66 days in a damaged sailboat off the Carolina coast. Louis Jordan left Conway, South Carolina in January to fish but was capsized by a storm that broke his mast and shoulder; he survived by collecting rainwater and catching fish attracted to his laundry. The container ship Houston Express spotted him signaling for help hundreds of miles from land, and he was airlifted to a Norfolk hospital in surprisingly good physical and mental condition.
